title: Repent a day before you die (Avot 2:10)
word: Repent a day before you die
hook: Rabbi Eliezer: repent one day before your death, and no one knows the day, so every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, five students, five answers, and the one that held all the others. Your line was a good heart. What did a good heart choose? Today, one of those students speaks. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Everybody has a someday list for the heart. Someday I'll call my brother and make it right. Someday I'll stop snapping at the people I love. Someday I'll say sorry for that thing in college. Someday is comfortable. It's always there, just past the horizon. Rabbi Eliezer, one of the five students from yesterday, the one whose memory was like a cistern that never lost a drop, gave three pieces of advice. The third one takes the word someday and quietly removes it.

Rabbi Eliezer said three things. Let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own. Don't be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. That last one sounds strange. How are you supposed to know which day that is? His students asked him exactly that, and the Talmud records his answer. Does anyone know the day he'll die? All the more reason to repent today, in case you die tomorrow. Then all your days will be spent in repentance. The word is teshuvah. It's usually translated repentance, but it really means return, or turning. You notice you've wandered off the path, and you turn back toward it. No groveling required, no drama. Just a turn. The Talmud then tells a parable. A king invited his servants to a banquet, but didn't say when. The wise ones dressed in their best and waited by the palace door. After all, a palace is never short of anything; the feast could start any minute. The foolish ones went off to their work, saying, there's no banquet without a lot of preparation first. Suddenly the king called them in. The wise walked in dressed and ready. The foolish came in dirty from work, and weren't allowed to sit at the table. The rabbis even find a verse for it, in Ecclesiastes, which in the old King James wording says, "Let thy garments be always white." Not out of fear. Just ready. Rabbi Eliezer's advice isn't gloomy. It's freeing. If today might be the day, then today is the day to turn.
screen: `THREE PIECES OF ADVICE.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE DAY.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `THE KING'S BANQUET.` · then, large: `LET THY GARMENTS BE ALWAYS WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one thing off the someday list. Settle, and breathe. Let the list come up. The call. The apology. The habit you keep meaning to drop. Pick just one. Now imagine it's the last day you'll have to do it. Not in a frightening way. Just clearly. What's the smallest turn you could make toward it today? A text. A sentence. Setting something down. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Repent a day before you die. Rabbi Eliezer's riddle: nobody knows the day, so turn back today, and every day is a day of teshuvah.
screen: `REPENT A DAY BEFORE YOU DIE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: repent today. Pick one thing off your someday list and make the first small turn toward it before you go to sleep. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats teshuvah, returning, as possible every day, not only on Yom Kippur, and many Jews include a moment of personal reckoning in their bedtime prayers.

original.note: Hebrew: repentance, literally a turning back.

trapdoor: what you thought: fix things before it's too late.
what it means: nobody knows the day, so turn back today, and every day becomes a day of return.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud reads Ecclesiastes 9:8, let thy garments be always white, as always being ready for the king's call.

sources.quoted: Let thy garments be always white

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:10 common, 2:15 in some editions.
Ecclesiastes 9:8 is quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 is believed to read the same for this clause but was not verified.

Shabbat 153a: the students' question, Eliezer's answer, and the parable of the king's banquet (told there in the name of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai); the script does not name the parable's teller; confirm.
'A cistern that never lost a drop' is Yochanan ben Zakkai's praise of Eliezer in Avot 2:8.
